title: The Archivist's Son: Avignon, Baltimore, and the Theory of the Victim
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Avenue de l'Arrousaire, Avignon: the birth on Christmas Day
stops.date_confidence: date and city attested by both Wikipedia editions of 'René Girard'; the street and the house are reconstruction only, from local Avignon family-history material carried in the working dossier, and the house does not survive. Coordinate corrected in verification: the pool's 43.9335, 4.8225 falls roughly 600 m outside the bounding box of avenue de l'Arrousaire; 43.9395, 4.8126 sits on the street itself per OSM. The full birth name, René Noël Théophile Girard, is given by both Wikipedia editions; the chronology lens had dropped the third name.
stops.campa: René Noël Théophile Girard is born on Christmas Day in a house on the Arrousaire road, at the southern edge of Avignon outside the walls. The full name carries two saints and a date, and the family will use only the first of the three. The natal house is demolished at some later point that nobody records, and what survives of the address is a street name and a tram stop. His father Joseph Girard is an archiviste-paléographe, trained at the École des chartes in Paris, and keeper of the city's antiquities.
suggested_refs: Avenue de l'Arrousaire, Avignon, and the Arrousaire tram stop, the surviving markers of an address whose house is gone
sources: OpenStreetMap / Nominatim, avenue de l'Arrousaire, Avignon

stops.name: Musée Calvet, Avignon: the father's keys
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to date and daily detail. Joseph Girard's Avignon curatorship is attested by the Académie française's own biographical page for his son, which names him curator of the Musée Calvet and an administrator of the Palais des Papes; the c. 1906-1949 span comes from the working dossier and was not confirmed against a museum record in this pass. The date 1928 is an ordering device for the childhood segment and marks nothing.
stops.campa: At 65 rue Joseph-Vernet, behind the front of a hôtel particulier, the Bibliothèque et Musée Calvet holds Avignon's paintings, its Greek bronzes, its herbarium, its coins and its books. Joseph Girard is its curator. René will spend four years at the École des chartes learning the same discipline and then leave the archive for the novel. Before any of that the boy has the run of the place: catalogues, accession numbers, objects with a provenance and objects without one, a household whose daily business is the custody of things other people made.
suggested_refs: The Bibliothèque et Musée Calvet, 65 rue Joseph-Vernet, Avignon, under Joseph Girard's curatorship
sources: academie-francaise.fr, 'Les Immortels: René Girard', biographical page
Working dossier, on Joseph Girard's curatorship c. 1906-1949 (unconfirmed against a museum record)

stops.name: Palais des Papes, Avignon: the fortress of the schism
stops.date_confidence: attested that Joseph Girard administered the Palais des Papes (academie-francaise.fr, biographical page for René Girard) and that the family lived in Avignon through his son's childhood; the date 1932 orders the segment and marks no event. The reading of the Avignon schism as formative is the writer's juxtaposition, not a claim Girard is anywhere on record making.
stops.campa: The papal fortress stands over the town, a wall of stone with almost no windows, thrown up in twenty years by popes who would not go back to Rome. Joseph Girard administers it. His son grows up inside a monument to a schism: two rival popes at once, two obediences, Christendom divided against itself over which of two men was the true one and each side certain. Girard will spend his working life on what a community does when it can no longer tell its rivals apart. Whether the fortress had anything to do with that is not a claim he is anywhere on record making.
suggested_refs: The Palais des Papes, Avignon, seat of the Avignon obedience during the Western Schism
sources: academie-francaise.fr, 'Les Immortels: René Girard', biographical page

stops.name: École nationale des chartes, Paris: entry under the occupation
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia, French, 'René Girard'): entered the École nationale des chartes in 1943 to train as an archivist-paleographer, during the German occupation. The school's address at 19 rue de la Sorbonne from 1897 to 2014 is confirmed by Wikipedia, 'École nationale des chartes'. Month unknown, defaulted to January. The description of the syllabus is general knowledge about the school's training, not a sourced account of his own coursework.
stops.campa: He enters the École nationale des chartes at 19 rue de la Sorbonne, in a Paris under German occupation, to be trained exactly as his father was: paleography, diplomatics, the criticism of charters, the discipline of telling a forged document from a real one. Nothing whatever in that syllabus concerns desire. What the training instils is a particular suspicion, that a text presents itself as evidence for something and may be lying about what. Bread is rationed. The school is very small.
suggested_refs: The École nationale des chartes at 19 rue de la Sorbonne, its address from 1897 to 2014

stops.name: École nationale des chartes, Paris: the thesis on private life in Avignon
stops.date_confidence: attested by both Wikipedia editions of 'René Girard': diploma thesis 'La vie privée à Avignon dans la seconde moitié du XVe siècle', completed 1947. The advisors Marcel Aubert and André Masson come from the working dossier's citation of the École's digital catalogue and were not independently reopened in this pass. Month unknown, defaulted to January.
stops.campa: His diploma thesis is titled La vie privée à Avignon dans la seconde moitié du XVe siècle: private life in his own city, in the century after the popes left it. He works through wills, inventories, marriage contracts and household accounts, the paper a town leaves behind when nothing in particular is happening to it. The diploma of archiviste-paléographe is a licence to spend a working life in a French reading room, and it is what his father did with his. He takes the diploma and leaves the country inside the year.
suggested_refs: 'La vie privée à Avignon dans la seconde moitié du XVe siècle', École nationale des chartes diploma thesis, 1947

segments.name: The One-Year Fellowship: Indiana, Duke, Bryn Mawr

stops.name: Indiana University, Bloomington: the fellowship that was to last a year
stops.date_confidence: attested by both Wikipedia editions of 'René Girard': left France in 1947 on a French government teaching fellowship to Indiana University, Bloomington, initially intended as a one-year stay. Month set to September for the academic year; the sources give the year only. The limited-English detail is from the working dossier.
stops.campa: He crosses on a French government teaching fellowship, one year, to Bloomington, Indiana, with limited English and no intention at all of staying. The Old Crescent is limestone and the town is small and flat. He teaches French to Americans who have lately come back from the war fought in his country. He will never hold a permanent university post in France, and will die an American resident. The one year becomes two, then a doctorate, then sixty-eight years.
suggested_refs: The Old Crescent and Sample Gates, Indiana University, Bloomington

stops.name: Indiana University, Bloomington: American Opinion of France
stops.date_confidence: 1950 attested by both Wikipedia editions of 'René Girard' for the PhD in history and the dissertation title 'American Opinion of France, 1940-1943'. The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy instead dates the Indiana doctorate to 1947; that contradiction is left standing rather than resolved, with 1950 used here because two independent language editions corroborate it. Month unknown, defaulted to January.
stops.campa: The dissertation is American Opinion of France, 1940-1943: what Americans thought of Vichy, of de Gaulle, of the country he had just left. The medievalist's tools are turned on newspapers, wire copy and propaganda, on what one public believes about a foreign nation and on who benefits from its believing that. He does not return to the Middle Ages as a subject again. The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy dates this doctorate to 1947 instead of 1950, and the disagreement has never been settled.
suggested_refs: René Girard, 'American Opinion of France, 1940-1943', PhD dissertation, Indiana University, 1950
sources: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'René Girard' (conflicting doctorate year, recorded not resolved)

stops.name: Bloomington, Indiana: the marriage to Martha McCullough
stops.date_confidence: date 18 June 1952 and spouse Martha McCullough attested (Wikipedia, French, 'René Girard', which further specifies she was an American librarian). The place of the ceremony is not given by any source reachable in this pass; the stop is pinned at Indiana, where he was then employed, and the pin should be read as an ordering device rather than a location. Children's birth years attested (Wikipedia, English). The working dossier's 'Methodist ceremony' detail could not be confirmed anywhere and is not stated as fact.
stops.campa: He marries Martha McCullough, an American librarian, on the eighteenth of June. Three children follow: Martin in 1955, Daniel in 1957, Mary in 1960. The marriage lasts sixty-three years and ends only at his death in California. He is at this point a French doctoral graduate with no permanent position, teaching language courses on renewable terms, in a country where he has no family and no career. The working dossier calls the ceremony Methodist; that detail is in no source reachable here and is set aside.
suggested_refs: fr.wikipedia's account of the marriage of 18 June 1952 to Martha McCullough, bibliothécaire américaine

stops.name: Indiana University, Bloomington: the departure nobody agrees about
stops.date_confidence: genuinely contested and left contested. en.wikipedia gives Indiana 1947-1953; fr.wikipedia gives Indiana 1947-1952 with Duke beginning 1952. The correct presentation is 1947 to 1952/53, not a flat 1953. Whether the departure was a non-renewal or a dismissal is unresolved in the biographical retellings cited by the working dossier, and no institutional personnel record has been located. Month unknown, defaulted to January.
stops.campa: He leaves Indiana. English Wikipedia gives his Bloomington years as 1947 to 1953; French Wikipedia ends them in 1952 and has him at Duke from that year. The biographical retellings differ further on what actually happened there: a contract quietly not renewed, or an outright dismissal. No institutional personnel record has been produced either way, and neither version is preferred here. He is twenty-nine, holds a doctorate in history, and has tenure nowhere. The next four years are spent moving.

stops.name: Duke University, Durham: French in the segregated South
stops.date_confidence: contested. fr.wikipedia gives Duke 1952-1953; en.wikipedia gives Duke and Bryn Mawr together as 1953-1957 without splitting the years. The working dossier's span of 1953-1955 is supported by neither source and is rejected here as an invented split. Month unknown, defaulted to January. The Cynthia Haven attribution is reconstruction from the dossier's citation of Evolution of Desire (2018) and was not reopened in this pass; Girard is not on record making the connection himself.
stops.campa: Duke University, in Durham, North Carolina, in the segregated South. He teaches French to undergraduates and watches a society hold itself together by a line drawn through its own population. The appointment is brief on every account, and the accounts disagree about how brief. His biographer Cynthia Haven links this period to his later attention to crowds and to the sudden unanimity of a town against one of its own. Girard himself says nothing of the kind anywhere reachable in this pass.
suggested_refs: Cynthia L. Haven, Evolution of Desire: A Life of René Girard (Michigan State University Press, 2018)

stops.name: Bryn Mawr College, Pennsylvania: the insecure years
stops.date_confidence: both Wikipedia editions give Bryn Mawr 1953-1957; the pool's 1955-1957 is unsupported and is corrected here. Coordinate corrected in verification: the pool's 40.0225, -75.3157 lies roughly 690 m south of the campus, in Bryn Mawr village near the rail line; OSM places Bryn Mawr College at 40.0287, -75.3155. Month set to June only to order the stop after the Duke entry; no month is given by any source. The claim about what he was reading in these years is inference backward from the 1961 book, not attested.
stops.campa: Bryn Mawr College, stone and gothic on the Main Line outside Philadelphia, a women's college where he is assistant professor of French. Martin is born in 1955. These are the insecure years: short contracts, a growing family, an accent, and a research subject he has not yet found. He is reading novels rather than archives, and beginning to notice that the characters in them do not appear to want anything on their own account. Johns Hopkins offers tenure in 1957 and he takes it.
suggested_refs: Bryn Mawr College Department of French faculty records, 1953-1957

segments.name: Baltimore: Tenure, Conversion, and the Colloquium

stops.name: Johns Hopkins University, Gilman Hall: tenure at last
stops.date_confidence: attested by both Wikipedia editions of 'René Girard': Johns Hopkins from 1957, full professor 1961, remaining until 1968. Daniel's birth year 1957 attested (Wikipedia, English). Month unknown, defaulted to January. Richard Macksey's presence and willingness to cross departmental lines is from the working dossier and from roland_barthes.journey.json; the characterization is the writer's.
stops.campa: Johns Hopkins, Baltimore, and tenure at last, in the Department of Romance Languages. Daniel is born the same year. Gilman Hall sits at the head of the Homewood quadrangle, and the Humanities Center that will make the place famous has not yet been founded. Girard finds colleagues willing to cross departmental lines, Richard Macksey above all. He is thirty-three, has been in the United States ten years, and has published no book. He will be here eleven years, leave for Buffalo, and come back to Baltimore for four more.
suggested_refs: Gilman Hall and the Homewood campus, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore

stops.name: Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore: the conversion at the desk
stops.date_confidence: attested that a conversion occurred while he was completing his first book, described afterwards as a return to Catholic practice, and that en.wikipedia frames it through his reading of Dostoevsky (Wikipedia, English, 'René Girard'). The precise date is given by no source in this pass and 1959 is an ordering device only. Separately: his two Guggenheim fellowships are given as 1959 and 1966 by en.wikipedia and as 1960 and 1967 by the working dossier, a one-year discrepancy on both, flagged rather than resolved.
stops.campa: Writing the last chapters of his first book, Girard undergoes what he afterwards calls a conversion: an intellectual one first, then a religious one, a return to the Catholic practice of his childhood. English Wikipedia frames it through his reading of Dostoevsky. He is finishing an argument that novelists discover, late and against their will, that their heroes' desires were never their own, and he says the same discovery happened to him at his own desk. A Guggenheim comes the same year, or the next; the sources differ. Mary is born in 1960.
suggested_refs: The conversion narrative as Girard told it in later interviews, dated only to the completion of Mensonge romantique
sources: Working dossier (Guggenheim years 1960 and 1967, conflicting with en.wikipedia's 1959 and 1966)

stops.name: Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore: Mensonge romantique et vérité romanesque
stops.date_confidence: attested by both Wikipedia editions of 'René Girard': Mensonge romantique et vérité romanesque, Grasset, Paris, 1961, introducing triangular or mimetic desire; full professor at Johns Hopkins the same year. Month unknown, defaulted to January. The roster of five novelists is the standard account of the book's contents and was not separately verified in this pass; only the Don Quixote line is quote-attested. Cervantes, Flaubert and Proust are named here as authors Girard read and wrote on, never as men he met.
stops.campa: Grasset publishes Mensonge romantique et vérité romanesque. The argument is a diagram: desire does not run in a line from a subject to an object, it runs in a triangle, subject to model to object, and what the subject actually wants is to be the model. Cervantes gives him the founding case, Don Quixote borrowing his desires wholesale out of Amadis of Gaul; the reading runs on through Stendhal, Flaubert, Proust and Dostoevsky. The romantic lie is that desire is spontaneous. Hopkins makes him full professor the same year.
stops.quote: The distance between Don Quixote and the petty bourgeois victim of advertising is not so great as romanticism would have us believe.
stops.quote_source: René Girard, Deceit, Desire and the Novel: Self and Other in Literary Structure, trans. Yvonne Freccero (Johns Hopkins University Press, 1965)
suggested_refs: Mensonge romantique et vérité romanesque (Grasset, 1961), translated as Deceit, Desire and the Novel (Johns Hopkins University Press, 1965)
sources: Girard, Deceit, Desire and the Novel, trans. Freccero (1965)

stops.name: Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore: Camus's Stranger retried
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The William Riley Parker Prize of the Modern Language Association for the essay 'Camus's Stranger Retried' is carried from the working dossier's citation of MLA prize records and was not independently confirmed on a fetched page in this pass. Month unknown, defaulted to January. The summary of the essay's argument is the writer's compression of a well-known piece, not a quoted claim, and Girard's own wording is not reproduced.
stops.campa: The Modern Language Association gives its William Riley Parker Prize to an essay called Camus's Stranger Retried. Girard reads L'Étranger as a trial staged by its own author: Meursault is condemned for the wrong reasons so that the reader will acquit him for the wrong reasons in turn, and the jury inside the book stands for a crowd that always knows in advance who is guilty. It is his first piece of work on a living reputation. Albert Camus had been dead five years when it appeared.
suggested_refs: René Girard, 'Camus's Stranger Retried', PMLA (1964), winner of the MLA William Riley Parker Prize
sources: Working dossier, citing MLA prize records (not independently confirmed in this pass)

stops.name: Johns Hopkins University, Homewood campus: the colloquium of October 1966
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day range. The colloquium ran 18 to 21 October 1966 at Johns Hopkins, organized by René Girard and Richard A. Macksey for the newly founded Humanities Center with Ford Foundation funding, and Derrida read his paper on 21 October (Wikipedia, 'Structure, Sign, and Play in the Discourse of the Human Sciences'). That source names Eugenio Donato as a co-editor of the proceedings rather than as a co-organizer, while fr.wikipedia's 'René Girard' names Donato as a third organizer; the discrepancy is recorded, not resolved. The title appears as both 'The Language of Criticism' and 'The Languages of Criticism' across sources. The participant list beyond Derrida is from the working dossier and from roland_barthes.journey.json.
stops.campa: Girard and Richard Macksey convene The Language of Criticism and the Sciences of Man at the new Humanities Center, on Ford Foundation money, to introduce French structuralism to American academics who have mostly not read any. Roland Barthes comes, and Jacques Lacan, and Jean Hyppolite, and Lucien Goldmann, and Tzvetan Todorov. On the twenty-first, Jacques Derrida reads Structure, Sign, and Play in the Discourse of the Human Sciences, which takes structuralism apart in front of a room still learning its name. Girard has organized the event that will be remembered for the paper against it.
suggested_refs: Richard Macksey and Eugenio Donato, eds., The Structuralist Controversy: The Languages of Criticism and the Sciences of Man (Johns Hopkins University Press, 1970)
sources: Wikipedia, 'Structure, Sign, and Play in the Discourse of the Human Sciences'

stops.name: Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore: the introduction, if it happened
stops.date_confidence: contested, and left contested. Both jacques_lacan.journey.json and jacques_derrida.journey.json carry this as one of two incompatible sourced accounts of the first Lacan-Derrida meeting; the other, Élisabeth Roudinesco's, gives Girard no part in it at all and runs on the Cartesian subject and the signifier instead. The Girard-introduction version traces to booksandtales.com in both atlas files and could not be independently confirmed in this pass; the working dossier does not mention it. Date set to 21 October 1966, the day of Derrida's paper, to order the segment.
stops.campa: One of the two accounts standing in the record has Girard himself making the introduction when Jacques Lacan and Jacques Derrida meet for the first time, at Baltimore, and the two of them talking about death and about how each expected to be read after his own. The same account reports Lacan telling Girard afterwards that the difference between himself and Derrida is that Derrida has nothing to do with people who suffer. The other account gives Girard no part in the meeting whatever. Which of the two is true has not been established.
suggested_refs: The two incompatible accounts of the first Lacan-Derrida meeting at Baltimore, one placing Girard as the introducer, the other (Roudinesco's) omitting him

segments.name: Buffalo and the Return to Baltimore: Violence and the Sacred

stops.name: SUNY Buffalo, South Campus: the second phase begins
stops.date_confidence: attested that he moved to the State University of New York at Buffalo in 1968 (Wikipedia, French, 'René Girard'). en.wikipedia gives no Buffalo dates at all, saying only that for several years he moved back and forth between Buffalo and Johns Hopkins; fr.wikipedia's span is 1968-1975, and the working dossier's 1968-1976 has no Wikipedia backing, so the discrepancy is dossier-versus-fr.wikipedia, not en-versus-fr. Coordinate corrected in verification: the pool's 42.937, -78.8256 is roughly 1.9 km south of the pre-Amherst campus; OSM places the South Campus at Main and Bailey at 42.9534, -78.8186. Month unknown, defaulted to January. The characterization of the Buffalo faculty is the writer's.
stops.campa: He moves to the State University of New York at Buffalo, to the South Campus at Main and Bailey, in the years when Buffalo is buying an interdisciplinary humanities faculty and then letting it do as it likes. Girard has stopped writing about novels. The second phase of the theory starts here: not borrowed desire, but what borrowed desire does to a crowd that has caught it. He is reading Greek tragedy, the ethnographic literature on sacrifice, and the accounts of what a town does to itself during a plague.
stops.quote: Because humans imitate one another, they have had to find a means of dealing with contagious similarity
stops.quote_source: René Girard, 'On War and Apocalypse,' First Things (August 2009); fragment of a longer sentence, fetched from firstthings.com

stops.name: SUNY Buffalo: La Violence et le sacré
stops.date_confidence: attested by both Wikipedia editions of 'René Girard': La Violence et le sacré, Grasset, Paris, 1972, presenting the scapegoat-mechanism hypothesis through myth, tragedy and ethnology. Month unknown, defaulted to January. The stop is pinned at Buffalo, where he was employed in 1972; no source places the writing at any particular desk. The Académie française's Prix Broquette-Gonin for the book in 1973 comes from the working dossier's citation of Académie prize records and was not reopened here. The quotation is sourced to the 1977 Johns Hopkins translation via a quotation database and its page number could not be confirmed.
stops.campa: The thesis of La Violence et le sacré is that violence inside a community is contagious and reciprocal, that vengeance answers vengeance without any natural stopping point, and that the way out human societies actually found was to discharge the whole of it onto a single victim who could not answer back. The killing works. The community is at peace afterwards and cannot account for why, so it calls the victim a god. Ritual is the rehearsal of the killing, prohibition the fence around it. Grasset publishes the book in Paris in 1972.
stops.quote: The goal of religious thinking is exactly the same as that of technological research -- namely, practical action.
stops.quote_source: René Girard, Violence and the Sacred, trans. Patrick Gregory (Johns Hopkins University Press, 1977)
suggested_refs: La Violence et le sacré (Grasset, 1972), translated as Violence and the Sacred (Johns Hopkins University Press, 1977)
sources: Girard, Violence and the Sacred, trans. Gregory (1977)

stops.name: Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore: the return, and the anthropologists
stops.date_confidence: attested that he returned to Johns Hopkins and remained until 1980 (Wikipedia, French, 'René Girard'). The pool gives 1976 for the return while fr.wikipedia's Buffalo span ends in 1975, leaving a year unaccounted for; the gap is recorded rather than filled. Month unknown, defaulted to January. The characterization of the anthropological reception is the writer's and is not a sourced claim; the 1977 Johns Hopkins University Press translation is attested by the edition cited elsewhere in this file.
stops.campa: He comes back to Baltimore. The English translation of Violence and the Sacred appears from the Johns Hopkins University Press in 1977, and the book begins to be argued about by anthropologists who had not asked a professor of French for a theory of sacrifice. He has done no fieldwork and reads none of the languages of the peoples he cites. He holds no standing whatever in the discipline about which he has just made a very large claim, and he acquires none in the forty years left to him.
suggested_refs: The Johns Hopkins University Press translation of Violence and the Sacred (1977) and its reception among professional anthropologists

stops.name: Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore: Des choses cachées depuis la fondation du monde
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia, English, 'René Girard'): published 1978 as a dialogue with the psychiatrists Jean-Michel Oughourlian and Guy Lefort, systematizing mimetic theory and giving it explicit Christian argument. Month unknown, defaulted to January. That the title quotes Matthew 13:35, and the claim that the book cost him secular readers, are the writer's additions and are not sourced in this pass.
stops.campa: Des choses cachées depuis la fondation du monde runs to book length as a conversation with two psychiatrists, Jean-Michel Oughourlian and Guy Lefort, who ask the questions and push back. The title is a line out of Matthew, and what the book costs him in secular readers no source counts. In it Girard makes the argument he had kept out of the previous book: that the Gospels describe the very mechanism the myths describe, but from the position of the victim rather than of the crowd, and that describing it from there breaks it.
stops.quote: There is no culture without a tomb and no tomb without a culture.
stops.quote_source: René Girard, Jean-Michel Oughourlian, and Guy Lefort, Things Hidden Since the Foundation of the World, trans. Stephen Bann and Michael Metteer (Stanford University Press, 1987)
suggested_refs: Des choses cachées depuis la fondation du monde (Grasset, 1978), translated as Things Hidden Since the Foundation of the World (Stanford University Press, 1987)
sources: Girard, Oughourlian and Lefort, Things Hidden, trans. Bann and Metteer (1987)

stops.name: Stanford University, Main Quad: the Andrew B. Hammond chair
stops.date_confidence: contested by one year. fr.wikipedia gives the Stanford appointment as 1980-1995; en.wikipedia says 1981 in both its body text and its appointment table, so the pool's claim that en.wikipedia's summary line and body disagree with each other is inaccurate and is corrected here. The real discrepancy is en=1981 against fr=1980. 1980 is used to order the segment. Month unknown, defaulted to January. The John Freccero detail is from the working dossier and was not independently confirmed.
stops.campa: Stanford makes him Andrew B. Hammond Professor of French Language, Literature, and Civilization. John Freccero, the Dante scholar and an old friend, had worked to bring him west. The French department has acquired a professor who will spend most of his time on anthropology, on scripture and on Shakespeare. Girard is fifty-six, and this is the last move of his career. He holds the chair fifteen years and stays in Palo Alto for thirty-five, until he dies there.

stops.name: Stanford University: Disorder and Order
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the conference is carried from the working dossier and was not reconfirmed against a Stanford conference archive in this pass. Month unknown, defaulted to January. The gloss on the conference's premise is the writer's.
stops.campa: Stanford hosts a conference called Disorder and Order, setting Girard's account of a community in crisis beside contemporary work on self-organization in physical and biological systems. The bridge is a single idea: that order can come out of a disturbance without anybody having designed it. It is the first of the interdisciplinary meetings that will keep clustering around him at Stanford for the next twenty-five years, most of them convened by other people and most without him on the programme. The conference itself is carried on the working dossier alone and was reconfirmed against no Stanford archive.
suggested_refs: The 1981 Stanford 'Disorder and Order' conference proceedings
sources: Working dossier (not reconfirmed against a Stanford archive in this pass)

stops.name: Stanford University: Le Bouc émissaire and Guillaume de Machaut
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia, English, 'René Girard'): Le Bouc émissaire, Grasset, Paris, 1982, developing stereotypes of persecution as a method for reading myth and opening with Guillaume de Machaut's account of plague-era persecution. Month unknown, defaulted to January. The enumeration of four stereotypes is the standard summary of the book and was not verified against the text in this pass. The quotation is from a later book, The One by Whom Scandal Comes, and is placed here for its subject, not as a quotation from Le Bouc émissaire.
stops.campa: Le Bouc émissaire opens with Guillaume de Machaut, who wrote in the 1340s that the Jews had poisoned the rivers and that God had then sent a plague. Girard's move is to believe the plague and disbelieve the poisoning, and to read the text as the persecutors' own account of a persecution they cannot see as one. Four marks give such a text away: a crisis, a crime that abolishes distinctions, a victim carrying a sign, and violence. Myths, he argues, are the same document with the victim already turned into a god.
stops.quote: Everywhere and always, when human beings either cannot or dare not take their anger out on the thing that has caused it, they unconsciously search for substitutes, and more often than not they find them.
stops.quote_source: René Girard, The One by Whom Scandal Comes, trans. M. B. DeBevoise (Michigan State University Press, 2014)
suggested_refs: Le Bouc émissaire (Grasset, 1982), translated as The Scapegoat (Johns Hopkins University Press, 1986); Guillaume de Machaut, Le Jugement du Roy de Navarre

stops.name: Stanford University: the argument with Burkert and Jonathan Z. Smith

stops.campa: A Stanford discussion puts Girard in a room with the classicist Walter Burkert and the historian of religions Jonathan Z. Smith, all three arguing about where ritual killing comes from.
